Server setups: on Linux and Windows they ask for the minimum client protocol version of a server that keeps its own access keys, or take it as -minClientProtocolVersion: 8, the oldest supported and the default, keeps the gate open to every app; 15 resists probes, and older apps cannot connect (owner, 2026-11-01). Enter keeps the server's own; a managed server takes it from its server profile, so the option is refused with -httpBaseUrl. The settings' own key is replaced where it is; settings without one get a ServerConfig first, which the server lays over its access manager's; settings with a ServerConfig of their own are their admin's to edit, and the setup stops before it changes anything. CHANGELOG.Server says so

HTTP/3: what the IP-blocking plan's build review still said only there is beside the code now - Kestrel counts a header's name and value without HTTP/3's 32 bytes per field, takes te's "trailers" case-sensitively and :protocol on any method; a drained GOAWAY connection stays open as RC3 keeps it, which the application's connection limit bounds; and only the tests see the engine's internals. Comments only

Parity: the uncontrolled burst shares are diagnostics, and the exact response bytes, FIN and error outcomes, error codes and their scope, and the controlled parser-first and response-first schedules stay the release gates. Kestrel RC3's own shares move with the host's scheduling: the same reference gave other shares on the Windows Server 2025 Desktop VM (2 vCPU) than on this PC, and matching one host's percentages is no protocol requirement. Six real-QUIC cases hold the application and require the exact uppercase-name and malformed-QPACK trailer errors from both servers, which the sampled presence stood for. protocol-15.md and the release checklist say so
